title: Capveon looks for infrastructure contracts before the bidding starts
summary: Capveon looks for infrastructure contracts before the bidding starts
body_markdown:
[Capveon](https://capveon.ai/) wants manufacturers and contractors to discover public infrastructure work while there is still time to understand how their products fit. Its software combines opportunity discovery with analysis of the engineering specifications and procurement documents that determine what a project actually needs.


The YC Fall 2026 company is starting with water and wastewater projects, heavy civil construction and industrial infrastructure. Its founders, Finn Lancaster and Brison Moorhead, see a problem that extends beyond finding another bid notice: the important information can appear long before a project formally goes out to tender.


Plans and specifications are spread across government agencies, procurement portals, engineering firms and capital-improvement documents. By the time a notice reaches a conventional opportunity list, design and specification decisions may already be well advanced.


Capveon says it can identify relevant projects earlier in that process, including opportunities years before a bid. The product then helps users interpret the requirements, track changes and organize the information needed to pursue the work through an award.


[Watch the original product introduction](https://youtu.be/xpwCDcgNo-E) .


For an equipment manufacturer, the useful question is whether a planned project calls for something it can supply. For a contractor, it is whether the technical requirements match its capabilities. A project title or short procurement description may not answer either question. Capveon's website emphasizes the plans, specifications and drawings that someone on the team would otherwise have to review.


That places the product between an opportunity feed and the working process of preparing a pursuit. The company describes monitoring addenda and project changes alongside the initial search. Information that was useful when a project first appeared may need to be revised as engineers and agencies update the documents.


The founders bring experience from sales and software startups. Lancaster previously worked at Harper and on search machine learning at Publix, according to his public YC profile. Moorhead was a founding account executive at Bonsai, later acquired by Zoom, and an early sales hire at Harper. His background also includes HubSpot.


Those backgrounds help explain the focus on turning discovery into a commercial workflow. Finding a possible project is only the beginning of a sale that can involve manufacturers, distributors, engineers and contractors, each with a different role and timeline.


Capveon's announcement doesn't disclose customer counts, contract values won through the platform or independently measured time savings. It also doesn't specify how completely it covers the many agencies and document sources involved. Customers assessing the system will need to examine the relevance and currency of the opportunities it returns.


The company describes energy and defense as possible future markets, but its initial focus is the infrastructure categories already named. It is seeking conversations with manufacturers, distributors and contractors pursuing government projects.


The central test is whether an early signal leads to a useful next action. A manufacturer doesn't just need to know that a water project exists. It needs to understand which requirements matter, how they are changing and where its equipment can enter the conversation.
